Tell
tĕl
v. (to relate or declare; also to number or count; rendering Hebrew caphar, nagad, Greek lego, eipon)
From Saxon tellan, to count or relate — the same root as tally. The older English keeps both senses, and Scripture uses them together: God tells the number of the stars, and His people tell what He has done.

Biblical Definition

Tell in the Authorized Version carries two senses that modern English has separated: to relate, and to count. The counting sense appears where God's knowledge is measured against man's: “He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names” (Psalm 147:4). The stars are not merely counted but named, and the psalm sets this beside His healing of the broken in heart. The same verb turns painful in the psalm of the cross, where the sufferer counts his own bones: “I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me” (Psalm 22:17). The relating sense is where duty lies. Our Lord commissions the healed man to a domestic testimony rather than a public ministry: “Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee” (Mark 5:19). And He makes telling the first step of church discipline, restricted deliberately to two people: “if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother” (Matthew 18:15). The object of that telling is stated plainly — not vindication, but a brother gained.

Webster 1828 Definition

To utter; to relate; to make known; also, to number or count. Scripture has God telling the number of the stars, the sufferer telling his bones, the healed man telling his friends what the Lord has done, and a wronged brother telling a fault alone.

expand to see more

TELL, v.t. [Sax. tellan, to count, to relate.] To utter; to express in words; to communicate to others; as, tell me the story.

2. To relate; to narrate; to rehearse particularly; as, to tell a tale.

3. To make known; to publish; to disclose; as, tell not this abroad.

4. To number; to count; to reckon; as, to tell money; the shepherd tells his sheep.

5. To inform; to give notice or intelligence to; as, tell him of his danger.

TELL, v.i. To give an account; to make report; also, to take effect; as, every blow tells.

Key Scripture

Psalm 147:4 — "He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names."

Psalm 22:17 — "I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me."

Mark 5:19 — "Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee."

Matthew 18:15 — "Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother."

Modern Corruption

Telling a brother his fault alone has been abandoned at both ends — either nothing is said at all, in the name of tolerance, or it is said to everyone but him, which Scripture calls talebearing rather than telling.

expand to see more

Matthew 18:15 prescribes a sequence that scarcely survives anywhere. The first step is private, restricted to two people, and aimed at gaining a brother rather than establishing a case. Modern practice departs in two directions at once. Some hold that saying anything at all is judgmental, and the fault goes unaddressed until it hardens; others say it freely to third parties, in confidence, as a prayer request, or online, which Scripture names as talebearing and whispering and treats among the sins that separate chief friends. Both are failures of the same command, and both leave the brother precisely where he was.

The counting sense carries its own corrective, and it is worth holding beside the other. Psalm 147:4 places God's telling of the stars in the middle of a psalm about His care for the broken in heart, so that the same knowledge which numbers and names the host of heaven is engaged with the wounds of particular people. That is the ground on which Mark 5:19 sends a delivered man home to his friends. The testimony required of him was not eloquence or scale but an account of what the Lord had done for him — a form of telling available to every believer and neglected in favour of forms that are not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew caphar (to count, to recount) holds both senses in one root; nagad (to declare, to make known) supplies the relating sense; Greek lego and eipon render the ordinary telling of the New Testament.

expand to see more

Hebrew caphar (H5608) — to count, to number, to recount; the root joining telling stars and telling news.

Hebrew nagad (H5046) — to declare, to make known, to tell; used of declaring God's works among the people.

Hebrew manah (H4487) — to number, to appoint; the counting verb behind numbering days and portions.

Greek lego (G3004) — to say, to speak, to tell; the ordinary verb of the Gospels.

Greek elegcho (G1651) — to convict, to reprove; the verb rendered “tell him his fault” in Matthew 18:15.

Usage

"“He telleth the number of the stars” — the counting God also heals the broken in heart."

"“Tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee” — testimony begins at home."

"“Tell him his fault between thee and him alone” — the aim is a brother gained."
